You already know how to choose an ending with a lookup table and a die. A computer can repeat the same procedure much faster. Does that mean you understand more, less, or just do less repetitive work?

## Engage: what would you automate?

```step
stage: predict
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You want to sample 1,000 endings. What should the computer do?"
  options: ["Repeat the dice-and-table procedure", "Decide whether every sentence is true", "Replace the need to understand the lookup table"]
  actual: "The computer can repeat the dice-and-table procedure. Repetition alone does not establish truth or replace understanding."
```

## Explore: manual versus automatic

```step
stage: run
check:
  type: question
  q: "The program picks a random integer from 1 to 6 and uses the same table as your die. What changed?"
  options: ["The assigned probabilities", "Who performs the repeated sampling", "The meaning of the words"]
  answer: 1
```

## Explore: run it many times

```step
stage: run
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#explore", height: 590 }
check: { type: board, text: "Run at least 100 automated samples.", when: "a >= 100" }
```

Work with a partner:
1. Make five selections manually using the dice table from the previous lesson.
2. On the interactive board, choose **Run 100** to automate the **same** lookup table. Optionally repeat with 1,000 draws. A spreadsheet or short program is an alternative.
3. Tally mat, chair and roof. Compare the proportions with the intended 3/6, 2/6 and 1/6. Explain why the proportions may differ.

If no digital tool is available, combine the results of several groups to approximate a larger sample.

## Explain: what was offloaded?

```step
stage: investigate
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which task has the computer taken over?"
      options: ["Generating random outcomes and applying the lookup repeatedly", "Deciding whether the model represents real language well", "Judging whether an output is appropriate"]
      answer: 0
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You press Run 1000 and see mat 51%, chair 33%, roof 16%. Which job did the computer NOT do?"
      options: ["Decide whether six made-up endings are a good model of real sentences", "Roll the die 1000 times", "Count each word"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It did roll 1000 times: that is the job you handed over.", "It did count: that is part of the job you handed over."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name what was automated and what judgement remains with me." }
```

### Identify the automated work

Name the repeated task the computer now performs.

### Identify the human judgement

Who still decides whether the model and examples suit the question?

### Reflect on what remains yours

Explain what has been delegated and what still requires understanding.

**Cognitive offloading** means using a tool to take over some mental work. Here the computer takes over repeated execution and counting. In other tasks, AI might also generate explanations or recommendations, shifting some processing and potentially judgement.

Offloading is not automatically helpful or harmful. If the goal is to **learn how sampling works**, doing it manually first can reveal the mechanism. If the goal is to **compare thousands of samples**, automation makes a different investigation possible.

## Elaborate: learning mode or performance mode?

```step
stage: modify
check:
  type: question
  q: "A student has never seen the lookup table but copies 1,000 generated words into an assignment. Which learning check is most useful?"
  options: ["Ask them to explain and perform a few selections without the computer", "Assume the large output proves understanding", "Ask them to generate 10,000 more words"]
  answer: 0
```

Discuss two goals: **learning mode** (build a capability you can demonstrate yourself) and **performance mode** (complete a task efficiently). The same tool may be appropriate in both, but what you need to do independently can differ.

## Evaluate: transfer

```step
stage: info
check:
  type: question
  q: "A new die table has four faces for 'yes' and two for 'no'. Without running a program, what is the probability of 'no'?"
  options: ["1/6", "2/6", "4/6", "6/6"]
  answer: 1
```

In your own words, answer both questions:
- What did the computer do for you?
- What would you still need to understand to check whether it did the right thing?

## Evaluate: where the table breaks

```step
stage: info
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Our table only has a row for 'The cat sat on the…'. What does it say comes after 'The dog sat on the…'?"
      options: ["Nothing: there is no row for that phrase, so it is stuck", "mat, because mat is the most common ending", "A random word from the cat row"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Mat is common after 'The cat sat on the…'. The table has nothing at all for 'dog'.", "The table never mixes rows. It only looks up the exact phrase, and 'dog' is not there."]
      explain: "A lookup table only works for phrases it has a row for. One new word and it is stuck."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A real chatbot can finish 'The dog sat on the…' even if it never saw that exact sentence. Which idea best explains how?"
      options: ["It has learned that words like 'dog' and 'cat' are used in similar ways", "It has a row for every sentence anyone could ever write", "It picks words completely at random"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "There are far too many possible sentences to store them all.", "Its replies usually make sense, so it is not picking at random."]
```

### Find the missing row

Our model is a **lookup table**. It has one row: the endings for "The cat sat on the…". Now look up "The dog sat on the…". What can the table do?

### How does a chatbot still answer?

Real models learn which things **behave alike** (dogs and cats both sit on mats), so they can handle inputs they have never seen. This is called **generalising**. The table only memorises. You will see how a model generalises in the next unit, with a fruit sorter.

## Learning with AI: direct the help you receive

Imagine you are learning to use the dice lookup table. You ask an AI assistant to **act as your tutor**. It replies:

- **Response A:** “The answer is 2/6. Copy that into your worksheet.”
- **Response B:** “How many die faces lead to the word? How many faces are there altogether?”
- **Response C:** “Divide the number of matching faces by six. There are two matching faces, so the answer is 2/6.”

Which response leaves the thinking you are practising to you? Could Response C be helpful at a different stage of learning? These are prepared examples, not a live AI.

If a tutor gives you the whole answer when you wanted to practise, you can say so: *“Please let me work out the next step before you explain.”* Asking doesn't guarantee it will listen, so notice what it actually does.

```step
stage: investigate
check:
  type: question
  q: "You asked an AI tutor for hints, but it gave you the complete answer straight away. Your goal is to learn the method. What is the best next step?"
  options: ["Ask it for one hint at a time, then try the next step yourself", "Copy the answer: you can learn it from reading later", "Ask it a harder question instead"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Reading an answer can feel like learning, but you haven't practised the method.", "A harder question doesn't help you learn this method."]
```

**Independent check:** without AI, use this new table: **1 = sun, 2–3 = rain, 4–6 = cloud**. What is the chance of rain? Explain how you worked it out. Then reflect: what did you hand over today, and what thinking did you keep?

**Important limitation:** this is a fixed, transparent sampling model. Modern LLMs do not generate text by simply rolling a die over a six-entry table; they use much more complex learned patterns and context.

**Kind of AI:** your generator is a tiny version of AI that **makes new content** (generative AI). Unit 2 meets a different kind: AI that learns to predict or sort.

```teacher
summary: Compare manual and automated sampling and identify what judgement
  remains with the learner.
time: 25
goals:
  - I can name the job the computer took over (rolling and counting) and the
    judgement that stayed with me.
  - "I can explain why 1,000 rolls get closer to 3 : 2 : 1 than ten rolls do."
  - I can choose help from an AI tutor that leaves the thinking I'm practising
    to me.
before: >
  Use the board as a transparent fixed-context model, not a miniature modern
  LLM. No AI account is required. The Explain it to me clip is an optional
  scaffold after prediction.

  The three prepared tutor responses model how apparently helpful AI can still
  over-assist. Response B is usually better for a first independent attempt, but
  scaffolding should adapt to the student. If your school allows it, you can
  demonstrate the same request in a school-approved assistant yourself; students
  do not need accounts, and no provider or study mode is required. Avoid
  entering personal student information.

  The "cognitive offloading" definition follows Lodge and Loble (2026), listed
  in the lesson's sources.
running:
  - "Engage: ask what the computer should and should not do before anyone
    presses Run."
  - "Explore: have students perform five manual rolls before pressing Run 100."
  - "Explain: separate the job handed over (rolling, counting) from the
    judgement kept (is this a good model?)."
  - "Learning with AI: the independent check uses a new table, so students
    cannot reuse the Evaluate answer."
struggle: Faster output does not establish understanding or truth.
stuck:
  - see: A student says the computer understands the sentence.
    ask: Exactly which steps did it perform?
    fix: "Return to the board and list them: pick a number, look it up, count.
      Nothing else."
support: Use the prepared examples, read the explanation aloud and repeat a small trial.
stretch: Explain where the toy model differs from a modern AI assistant.
leads: Unit 2 moves from generating text to how AI learns from examples.
exit:
  q: What must you still understand after automating the rolls?
  a: How the six faces map to words, what the results mean, and how to judge
    whether the model suits the task.
explain: >
  The computer can repeat the same die-and-table procedure quickly. Running a
  hundred or a thousand trials gives more data to compare, but it does not make
  the words true or the model suitable. We can delegate repetitive execution
  while retaining judgement about the model and checking our own understanding.
  When an AI tutor over-helps, ask it for one hint at a time.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If the computer can do the rolling, is there any point in learning to do it
      by hand?
    prompts:
      - What did rolling by hand teach you that a percentage on the screen
        doesn't?
      - When would you just let the computer do it?
    notes: Both views are reasonable. Doing it by hand builds the understanding you
      need to check the computer's output; once you have that, handing over the
      repetition is sensible.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: discussion
      title: Who does which job?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Write three cards: build the table, roll the die, judge the result. Put
        each card on the 'me' or 'computer' side of your desk for 1,000 rolls,
        then explain one choice to a partner.
      notes: Most will hand over rolling. Ask whether anyone handed over judging, and
        why that would be risky.
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Race the computer
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        One half of the room rolls a die for 60 seconds and tallies; the other
        half watches the board run 1,000 times. Compare the two tallies.
      notes: "The computer is faster and closer to 3 : 2 : 1. Neither tally says
        whether 'The cat sat on the roof' is true."
    - at: modify
      kind: discussion
      title: Learning mode or performance mode?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Read out two situations: learning how probability works, and needing
        1,000 samples for a chart. Stand left for 'do it myself', right for
        'hand it over', for each.
      notes: The answer changes with the goal. Name this as the idea students will
        meet again in 'Decide what to hand over'.
```
